reason: The introduction suggests another body collides with the young world, and planetesimals are the available bodies.
expectation: The impact will produce material that can gather into a moon.

effect: The impact has thrown material into orbit, suggesting gravity can gather it into a moon.
reaction: The connection to the leading explanation for our Moon is satisfying, especially with its uncertainty acknowledged.
reason: Gravity is the natural next ingredient for gathering the orbiting debris.
expectation: Gravity will gather the impact debris toward forming a moon.

effect: Gravity gathered the impact debris into a Moon, completing the first goal; the remaining goal is to make a changing shore.
reaction: The impact-to-moon sequence was clear and satisfying.
reason: Water and the stone crust are the most direct visible ingredients for a sea and shore.
expectation: Water will collect against the crust to create a sea or shore.

effect: Water combined with the Moon automatically to make tides, suggesting they are needed for the changing shore.
reaction: I was surprised the tides came before a sea, though the Moon's gravitational role is clear.
reason: Tides acting on the stone crust suggest a shore that changes with the water.
expectation: The tides will shape or create a changing shore.

effect: Tides became Lunar rhythm rather than a shore, so I need to find another route to the sea or coast.
reaction: I didn't expect the Moon to be needed again, and Lunar rhythm's role is not yet clear.
reason: The stone crust seems relevant to a shore, but my direct attempt failed, so its compatibility list should help.
expectation: The inspection will reveal what can turn the crust into part of a shore.

effect: Stone crust currently has no available combinations, so it cannot provide the shore directly.
reaction: That is surprising given the shore goal, and leaves Lunar rhythm's purpose unclear.
reason: Lunar rhythm is the newest result, so checking its partners may reveal the next step toward the changing shore.
expectation: Its compatibility list will show how it contributes to the shore.

effect: Lunar rhythm has no available partners, so it does not currently reveal the route to the shore.
reason: Water at the rocky world is a plausible way to make the sea mentioned in the introduction.
expectation: Water will help form a sea on the planet.

alternatives.reason: I could check the hotspot's available ingredients first.

reaction: The route to the shore is still unclear.
reason: Inspecting the rocky world may reveal which available ingredient can advance the shore goal.
expectation: The hotspot will list any ingredients currently usable there.

effect: The rocky world accepts Mist and Air, giving me two possible routes toward the sea.
reaction: The hotspot list clarifies where to try next, though neither outcome is certain.
reason: Mist is water in the atmosphere, so it plausibly helps supply the cooling world with a sea.
expectation: Mist will contribute water to the planet, perhaps forming an ocean.

alternatives.reason: Air might establish an atmosphere before water gathers.

effect: Mist at the rocky world became First rain, suggesting the next step is to collect that water on the planet.
reaction: The condensation explanation makes the route to a sea clearer.
reason: First rain falling on the rocky world could collect into an ocean.
expectation: The rain will gather on the planet to form a sea or ocean.

effect: First rain collected in existing hollows in the crust; those hollows may lead to a sea.
reaction: The distinction between collecting rain and excavating ocean basins is helpful.
reason: Rain-filled hollows are the newest step toward a sea, but their next partner is not obvious.
expectation: Its available partners will indicate how the collected water develops into a sea.

effect: Water filled the hollows to form an Ocean, so the remaining task is to make its shore change.
reaction: The rain-to-ocean sequence now makes sense.
reason: The lunar rhythm and ocean together suggest the tidal movement needed for a changing shore.
expectation: The lunar rhythm will give the ocean a periodically changing shore.

effect: Ocean cannot combine with Lunar rhythm, but its available partners include Tides and Air.
reaction: I had assumed Lunar rhythm would drive the shore, so the distinction from Tides is a little unclear.
reason: Tides are the listed partner most directly associated with a shore that changes as water rises and falls.
expectation: The tides will create a periodically changing shore along the ocean.

alternatives.reason: Air might also change the ocean's shore, perhaps through waves.

effect: Ocean and Tides made a Tidal shore, completing the remaining goal.
reaction: The advancing and retreating water makes a satisfying ending to the shore sequence.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making rain-filled hollows was most worthwhile: it connected the mythic sequence to the useful distinction that rain collects in existing low places rather than excavating ocean basins by itself.

leastWorthwhile.text: Inspecting Stone crust and Lunar rhythm yielded no partners, leaving the route to the sea unclear and slowing progress.

surprise.text: Water and the Moon produced Tides before there was an Ocean; later, Lunar rhythm could not be used in place of Tides to make the shore.

arbitrary.text: Combining Tides with the Moon again to produce Lunar rhythm felt arbitrary: its purpose was unclear, and it did not work in my attempt to make the shore.

continue.text: Yes. I would be curious to see what the world makes next: the impact-to-moon and rain-to-ocean sequences combined evocative creation with useful scientific qualifications, despite some unclear recipes.
